Indiana 'religious freedom' law raises discrimination fears

INDIANAPOLIS — Hundreds of people, some carrying signs reading “no hate in our state,” gathered Saturday outside the Indiana Statehouse for a boisterous rally against a new state law that opponents say could sanction discrimination against gay people or minority religions.

Since Republican Gov. Mike Pence signed the bill into law Thursday, Indiana has been widely criticized by businesses and organizations around the nation, as well as on social media with the hashtag #boycottindiana. Local officials and business groups around the state hope to stem the fallout, although consumer review service Angie’s List said Saturday that it is suspending a planned expansion in Indianapolis because of the new law.

The law’s supporters contend discrimination claims are overblown and insist it will keep the government from compelling people to provide services they find objectionable on religious grounds. They also maintain that courts haven’t allowed discrimination under similar laws covering the federal government and 19 other states.

But state Rep. Ed DeLaney, an Indianapolis Democrat, said Indiana’s law goes further than those laws and opens the door to discrimination.

“This law does not openly allow discrimination, no, but what it does is create a road map, a path to discrimination,” he told the crowd, which stretched across the south steps and lawn of the Statehouse. “Indiana’s version of this law is not the same as that in other states. It adds all kinds of new stuff and it moves us further down the road to discrimination.”

The measure, which takes effect in July, prohibits state laws that “substantially burden” a person’s ability to follow his or her religious beliefs. The definition of “person” includes religious institutions, businesses and associations.

David Sklar, of the Indianapolis Jewish Community Relations Council told, also spoke out against the law .

“It’s ambiguity, gray area that is created in this legislation will ultimately hurt the Jewish community more than it will help it,” he told local news outlet WISH.

Muslim and Hindu officials have also expressed worries that the law could be used to discriminate against them on religious grounds.

Saturday’s crowd, for which police didn’t have an exact estimate, chanted “Pence must go!” several times and many people held signs like “I’m pretty sure God doesn’t hate anyone” and “No hate in our state.”

Zach Adamson, a Democrat on Indianapolis’ City-County Council, said to cheers that the law has nothing to do with religious freedom but everything to do with discrimination.

“This isn’t 1950 Alabama; it’s 2015 Indiana,” he told the crowd, adding that the law has brought embarrassment on the state.

Angie’s List had sought an $18.5 million incentive package from Indianapolis’ City-County Council to add 1,000 jobs over five years. But founder and CEO Bill Oseterle said in a statement Saturday that the expansion was on hold “until we fully understand the implications of the freedom restoration act on our employees.”

Among those who attended the rally was Jennifer Fox, a 40-year-old from Indianapolis who was joined by her wife, Erin Fox, and their two boys, ages 5 and 8, and other relatives.

Fox said they married last June on the first day that same-sex marriage became legal in Indiana under a federal court ruling. She believes the religious objections law is a sort of reward to Republican lawmakers and their conservation Christian constituents who strongly opposed allowed the legalization of gay marriage in the state.

“I believe that’s where this is coming from — to find ways to push their own agenda, which is not a religious agenda; it’s aimed at a specific section of people,” Fox said.

Although many Indianapolis businesses have expressed opposition to the law and support for gays and lesbians, Fox worries her family could be turned away from a restaurant or other business and that her sons would suffer emotionally.

“I certainly would not want them to think that there’s something wrong with our family because we’re a loving family,” she said.

Indianapolis Mayor Greg Ballard, a Republican who opposed the law, said he and other city officials would be talking to many businesses and convention planners to counter the uproar the law has caused. “I’m more concerned about making sure that everyone knows they can come in here and feel welcome,” Ballard said.

The Indianapolis-based NCAA has expressed concerns about the law and has suggested it could move future events elsewhere; the men’s Final Four will be held in the city next weekend.

Times of Israel staff contributed to this report

webpage.text:
Religious Freedom Laws in Indiana, Arkansas Create GOP Dilemma

Presidential hopefuls are caught in a battle between business and social conservatives.

Doug McSchooler|AP

Opponents rally against Indiana's Religious Freedom Restoration Act on the Indiana Statehouse lawn on March 28.

Former President Bill Clinton signed a version of it in 1993, with strong bipartisan support. Then-Illinois state Sen. Barack Obama voted for one in 1998. By early this year, 19 states had followed with their own statutes.

But with the 2016 presidential campaign looming and the issue of gay rights having taken a dramatic turn in public opinion, the Religious Freedom Restoration Act has become a political headache for Republicans and a base-building opportunity for Democrats, who say new laws don’t protect religious freedom so much as they imperil the rights of others.

The federal law (along with, analysts say, most of the state laws) was intended to have a fairly narrow but critical impact ensuring religious freedom. So people whose religions require them to cover their heads could do so in government ID photos, even if the rules dictate no hats. Native Americans would have their religious practices protected by law, and a Muslim prison guard could claim the right to wear a beard, as his religion dictates, despite the norm at his workplace. But laws initially signed in Indiana and passed by the legislature this week in Arkansas have critics worrying about a more sweeping impact, one in which people could refuse service or tenant housing to gays and lesbians, on the theory that the proprietors’ religion does not accept same-sex relationships.

The matter started heating up after Indiana Republican Gov. Mike Pence signed his state’s version of the RFRA in late March. As originally written and passed, the Indiana law, unlike other statutes, would apply even when the government is not a player, making its potential impact far more sweeping and dangerous to lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people, says Sarah Warbelow, an attorney with the Human Rights Campaign, which advocates for equal rights for LGBT people. Further, the law allows a company to be a “person” under the law, asserting a corporate religious belief even if the institution is not religious in nature. That, Warbelow says, opens the door to landlords refusing to rent to same-sex couples or even restaurants refusing to serve a transgender person.

“Sadly, over the years, the purpose of RFRA has been turned on its head,” she says.

The potential damage to GOP presidential hopefuls had already been done, forcing the contenders to choose between their social conservative base and the business community, which serves as a critical fundraising base. The initial response shows that GOP contenders have Iowa and its conservative Republican voters on their mind, says Charles Franklin, a Wisconsin-based pollster. Iowa’s Republican caucus electorate is on the conservative side – even more so than New Hampshire and South Carolina, other early primary states, he says, and with such a crowded emerging field, GOP contenders are eager to reach out to social conservatives.

The emergence and ensuing power of the tea party – a group more focused on small government and limited spending than on social issues – had pushed such matters as gay marriage and abortion aside, Franklin notes. But now – especially with a recovering economy moving that issue down as the major one concerning voters – social conservatives see an opportunity to get their causes back in the forefront.

“You’re seeing the candidates recognizing and responding to that wing of the party, coming back to the social and religious principles social and religious conservatives had prior to the emergence of the tea party,” Franklin says. What’s unclear, he adds, is whether it’s a function of ideology or a strategy to woo that segment of the party.

Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, so far the only announced GOP presidential contender, pointedly revealed his candidacy at Liberty University, a conservative Christian school, and this week denounced businesses for “listening to the extreme left-wing agenda” on the RFRA legislation. Kentucky Sen. Rand Paul last week addressed a prayer breakfast inside the Capitol Hill Club and urged ministers to fight the “moral crisis” that has led to the acceptance of gay marriage.

And after Pence signed Indiana’s pre-tweaked RFRA law, potential candidates including Florida Sen. Marco Rubio, physician Ben Carson, former Pennsylvania Sen. Rick Santorum and Louisiana Gov. Bobby Jindal piped in with words of praise. Perhaps most telling were the supportive comments by former Florida Gov. Jeb Bush, who is the most likely establishment choice among the contenders.

In Iowa, the GOP electorate includes libertarians and fiscal hawks along with social conservatives, says Tim Hagle, a University of Iowa political science professor. And candidates indeed need to “check the box” on certain issues to pass muster with voters in the caucuses. The RFRA issue may cut differently, he says, since people who are OK with gay marriages in which they have no part might not believe they have to “participate” by baking the wedding cake, for example.

Mark Graul, a Wisconsin-based GOP consultant, says the furor will likely die down after the primary season is over – or even before then. While Democrats, including Hillary Clinton and Martin O’Malley, have slammed the new RFRA legislation as discriminatory, such comments will rally the bases on both sides but not survive to the general election, he adds.

“When all is said and done, come next October, my assumption is we’re not going to be talking about social issues. We’ll be talking about national security and the economy,” Graul says.

But this is not 1993, when the federal RFRA was signed, or even 2004, when Democratic presidential nominee John Kerry tangled – inelegantly – with the question of whether the government should refuse to recognize same-sex unions, then an unpopular idea. Now, a majority of Americans support gay marriage – 59 percent, according to a recent Wall Street Journal/NBC poll, up from 30 percent in 2004. Young people in particular – including Republican youth – back gay marriage and could become an electoral problem for candidates who oppose it.

Arkansas Gov. Asa Hutchinson has firsthand experience with that. He announced Wednesday he would not sign Arkansas’ initial RFRA bill, and prodded the legislature to make changes to it.

One of the motivators? His own son, Seth, signed a petition asking that he veto the measure.

Religious Protection Laws, Once Called Shields, Are Now Seen as Cudgels

Politics|Religious Protection Laws, Once Called Shields, Are Now Seen as Cudgels

https://www.nytimes.com/2015/03/31/us/politics/religious-protection-laws-once-called-shields-are-now-seen-as-cudgels.html

You have a preview view of this article while we are checking your access. When we have confirmed access, the full article content will load.

When the federal government adopted a religious protection act in 1993, same-sex marriage was not on the horizon.

An informal coalition of liberals and conservatives endorsed the Religious Freedom Restoration Act because it seemed to protect members of vulnerable religious minorities from punishment for the exercise of their beliefs. The federal legislation was set off by a case in which two followers of the Native American church were fired and denied unemployment benefits because they took part in ceremonies with peyote, an illegal drug.

Twenty states, including Indiana last week, have since passed their own versions of religious freedom laws.

But over time, court decisions and conservative legal initiatives started to change the meaning of those laws, according to liberal activists. The state laws were not used to protect minorities, these critics say, but to allow some religious groups to undermine the rights of women, gays and lesbians or other groups.

“The coalition broke apart over the civil rights issues,” said Eunice Rho, a lawyer for the American Civil Liberties Union. The organization, which initially supported the measures, now opposes them unless they include language ensuring that they will not be used to permit discrimination or harm.

In the 1990s, for example, in the kind of case that raised red flags for civil rights advocates, landlords cited religious beliefs, sometimes with success in court, after refusing to rent to unmarried heterosexual couples.

INDIANAPOLIS — Hundreds of people gathered outside of the Indiana Statehouse on Saturday, some carrying "no hate in our state" signs, to rally against a new law that opponents say could sanction discrimination against gay people.

The law's supporters, however, contend the discrimination claims are overblown and insist it will keep the government from compelling people to provide services they find objectionable on religious grounds. Since Republican Gov. Mike Pence signed the bill into law Thursday, Indiana has been widely criticized by businesses and organizations around the country, as well as on social media with the hashtag #boycottindiana.

Local officials and business groups around the state hope to stem the fallout, though consumer review service Angie's List said Saturday that it is suspending a planned expansion in Indianapolis because of the new law. And Seattle Mayor Ed Murray prohibited the use of city government funds for city employees to travel to Indiana because of the law. "Seattleites know that discrimination has no place in our City — that's just equality '101'," Murray said in a statement.

The measure, which takes effect in July, prohibits state laws that "substantially burden" a person's ability to follow his or her religious beliefs. The definition of "person" includes religious institutions, businesses and associations.

Saturday's crowd stretched across the south steps and lawn of the Statehouse building. At one point, they chanted "Pence must go," and many held signs like "I'm pretty sure God doesn't hate anyone" and "No hate in our state." And stickers touting "This business serves everyone" have been appearing in many businesses' windows.

The Indianapolis-based NCAA has expressed concerns about the law and has suggested it could move future events elsewhere; the men's Final Four will be held in the city next weekend.

Indiana Governor Mike Pence defends religious freedom law – The Denver Post

INDIANAPOLIS — Indiana Gov. Mike Pence defended the new state law that’s garnered widespread criticism over concerns it could foster discrimination against gays and lesbians and said Sunday it wasn’t a mistake to have enacted it.

Pence appeared on ABC’s “This Week with George Stephanopoulos” to discuss the measure he signed last week prohibiting state laws that “substantially burden” a person’s ability to follow his or her religious beliefs. The definition of “person” includes religious institutions, businesses and associations.

Pence did not answer directly when asked at least six times whether under the law it would be legal for a merchant to refuse to serve gay customers. “This is not about discrimination, this is about empowering people to confront government overreach,” he said.

He was adamant that the measure will stick. “We’re not going to change this law,” he said. The Associated Press

jsonld.headline: Indiana Governor Mike Pence defends religious freedom law
creator: The Denver Post

resultats_lens.texte_contexte: Le gouverneur de l'Indiana, Mike Pence, a défendu la nouvelle loi sur la liberté religieuse lors d'une émission sur ABC (« This Week with George Stephanopoulos »), affirmant qu'elle ne visait pas à discriminer les homosexuels et les lesbiennes, mais à protéger les citoyens contre l'ingérence du gouvernement. La loi, signée la semaine précédente, interdit aux lois étatiques de « peser de manière substantielle » sur la capacité d'une personne à suivre ses convictions religieuses, englobant les institutions religieuses, les entreprises et les associations.

OTHER: Indiana s new religious freedom law
